name: Dravet Syndrome
description: Severe, treatment-resistant epilepsy caused by SCN1A mutations; onset in first year with prolonged febrile seizures, cognitive decline, and multiple seizure types.

frequency.sources: Orphanet: birth prevalence avg 1/30,000 (range 1/15,000–40,000). US Kaiser Permanente study (Wu et al., Pediatrics 2015) confirmed incidence 1/15,700. Atlas birth incidence within confirmed range.

diagnosis: Clinical criteria (fever-triggered hemiclonic seizures <1yr) + SCN1A genetic panel; Dravet-specific gene panel if SCN1A negative

treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Zorevunersen (STK-001; Stoke Therapeutics) —
antisense oligonucleotide targeting SCN1A NMD; Phase 3
EMPEROR study ongoing (NCT05237713); ETX101 (Encoded
Therapeutics) — AAV9-based SCN1A gene regulation; FDA
Breakthrough Therapy designation granted January 12, 2026;
first gene therapy candidate for Dravet Syndrome

name: Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS)
description: Severe childhood epilepsy with multiple seizure types, characteristic EEG pattern, and intellectual disability; often evolves from West syndrome.

frequency.sources: Orphanet: incidence 0.1– 0.28/100K/yr; prevalence at age 10 = ~2.6/10,000 children (Orphanet). Sullivan et al. 2024 systematic review (Epilepsia) confirmed prevalence 5.8–60.8/100K. Atlas rate of 2–3/100K consistent with Orphanet central estimate.

diagnosis: EEG (slow spike-wave <2.5Hz + paroxysmal fast activity) + clinical triad; MRI for structural causes; genetic panel

treatment.standardOfCare:
Valproate, clobazam, rufinamide, lamotrigine,
topiramate; VNS; corpus callosotomy
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Cannabidiol (Epidiolex) FDA 2018; fenfluramine
(Fintepla) FDA 2022

name: West Syndrome / Infantile Spasms
description: Epileptic encephalopathy of infancy with spasms, hypsarrhythmia on EEG, and developmental regression; onset 3–12 months.

frequency.global: ~460,000 – ~1.1M ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED]: Incidence 2–3.5/10,000 live births confirmed across multiple

diagnosis: EEG hypsarrhythmia (modified or classic); MRI brain; metabolic workup; chromosomal microarray + epilepsy gene panel

treatment.standardOfCare:
ACTH (Acthar Gel) FDA approved; vigabatrin (Sabril)
FDA 2009; prednisolone
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: TSC-related: vigabatrin preferred; ketogenic diet
adjunct trials

name: CDKL5 Deficiency Disorder
description: X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder with early-onset seizures, severe intellectual disability, and limited hand use; caused by CDKL5 gene mutations.

frequency.sources: Orphanet (Scotland): birth prevalence 1/42,400. IFCR: 1/40,000– 60,000. Atlas rate 1/40,000–60,000 confirmed.

diagnosis: CDKL5 gene sequencing + deletion/duplication; EEG; clinical criteria (early-onset seizures + Rett-like features)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Symptomatic ASMs (valproate, clobazam);
multidisciplinary supportive care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Ganaxolone (Ztalmy) FDA 2022 for CDD ages 2+;
disease-modifying trials ongoing

name: KCNQ2 Epilepsy
description: Neonatal-onset epilepsy caused by KCNQ2 potassium channel mutations; ranges from benign neonatal seizures to severe epileptic encephalopathy.

frequency.global: ~1,400 – ~2,800 Insufficent Data : Estimates based on: No firm population prevalence established. GeneReviews (NCBI) describes phenotypic spectrum but no prevalence figure. US urban study (PMC 2024) yielded minimum estimate 1/81,800 pre- genetic testing era. Atlas 1/50,000– 100,000 is reasonable but unconfirmed.

diagnosis: KCNQ2 gene sequencing (de novo variants); EEG (burst suppression neonatal); neonatal seizure presentation

treatment.standardOfCare:
Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine (Na+ channel blockers
preferred); phenobarbital
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Gene-specific clinical trials ongoing; ezogabine (no
longer available)

name: SCN8A Epilepsy
description: Early-onset epileptic encephalopathy with multiple seizure types caused by gain- of-function SCN8A sodium channel mutations; often drug- resistant.

frequency.global: ~23,000 – ~46,000 Insufficent Data : Estimates based on: No established population prevalence. ~550 patients diagnosed globally as of 2024 per The Cute Syndrome Foundation. Atlas 1/50,000–100,000 is an approximation; true prevalence likely underestimated due to recent recognition (gene identified 2012).

diagnosis: SCN8A gene sequencing; EEG; early- onset severe epilepsy phenotype

treatment.standardOfCare:
Sodium channel blockers (phenytoin, carbamazepine,
lacosamide)
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Quinidine in gain-of-function variants; no FDA
approval; Phase 2 trials

name: SCN2A Epilepsy
description: Variable epilepsy spectrum from benign neonatal seizures to severe epileptic encephalopathy; caused by SCN2A sodium channel mutations.

frequency.global: ~23,000 – ~46,000 Insufficent Data : Estimates based on: No established population prevalence. SCN2A is second most common sodium channel epilepsy gene after SCN1A per PMC review. Atlas 1/50,000–100,000 is an approximation; emerging condition with rapidly expanding case count.

diagnosis: SCN2A gene sequencing; distinguish gain-of-function (early-onset) vs loss-of- function (late-onset ASD/seizure)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Na+ channel blockers for GoF early-onset (phenytoin,
carbamazepine); avoid for LoF
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Precision genotype-based trials; no approved
therapy

name: PCDH19 Epilepsy
description: X-linked epilepsy affecting females with clustered febrile and afebrile seizures, social/behavioral issues, often with intellectual disability.

frequency.sources: PCDH19 epilepsy affects ~1/50,000 females; rare in males. Atlas confirmed. Brain (Oxford) 2019 population study (Symonds et al.) identified PCDH19 as one of most common genetic epilepsies in females.

diagnosis: PCDH19 gene sequencing (X-linked, affects heterozygous females); EEG; clinical pattern (fever-triggered cluster seizures)

treatment.standardOfCare: Clobazam; seizure management; supportive care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Ganaxolone trials (progesterone-based); no FDA-
approved specific therapy

name: Doose Syndrome (Myoclonic- Atonic Epilepsy)
description: Childhood epilepsy with myoclonic and atonic ('drop') seizures, normal early development; often treatment- resistant.

frequency.sources: Doose syndrome: 1–2% of childhood epilepsies; ~1–2/100K confirmed in multiple series. US urban population study (PMC 2024): incidence 1/34,100 (approx. 2.9/100K). Atlas estimate consistent.

diagnosis: Clinical (myoclonic-atonic seizures age 1–5, normal early development) + EEG (generalized 2–3Hz SW); gene panel to exclude specific DEEs

treatment.standardOfCare:
Valproate, ethosuximide, lamotrigine, clobazam;
ketogenic diet highly effective
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Avoid carbamazepine/vigabatrin; personalized
genetic counseling

name: Ohtahara Syndrome
description: Earliest-onset epileptic encephalopathy with suppression-burst EEG; onset in first weeks of life; severe prognosis.

frequency.sources: Ohtahara syndrome: <1/100,000 newborns. US urban study confirmed incidence 1/32,700 (~3/100K early infantile DEE, includes Ohtahara). Atlas rate confirmed.

diagnosis: EEG burst-suppression pattern; neonatal onset; MRI; comprehensive gene panel (STXBP1, SCN2A, KCNQ2, ARX, CDKL5)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Phenobarbital; ACTH; vigabatrin; multidisciplinary
palliative care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No proven disease-modifying therapy; very poor
prognosis

name: Aicardi Syndrome
description: X-linked dominant condition in females with infantile spasms, corpus callosum agenesis, and chorioretinal lacunae.

frequency.sources: Aicardi syndrome: ~1/100,000–167,000 females. US urban study: 1/71,600 (Aicardi with seizures). Atlas rate confirmed.

diagnosis: Clinical triad: infantile spasms + corpus callosum agenesis + chorioretinal lacunae; MRI; ophthalmology; affects females only

treatment.standardOfCare:
ACTH/vigabatrin for infantile spasms; multidisciplinary
supportive care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy; gene therapy
preclinical

name: Rasmussen Encephalitis
description: Rare progressive unihemispheric inflammatory disorder causing drug-resistant focal seizures, hemiplegia, and cognitive decline.

frequency.sources: Rasmussen encephalitis: US urban study confirmed ~1/450,000, consistent with ~500 total US cases. Atlas estimate confirmed.

diagnosis: MRI progressive hemispheric atrophy; EEG continuous unilateral slowing; brain biopsy (T-cell infiltrate); anti- GluR3/anti-GluA3 antibodies

treatment.standardOfCare: Functional hemispherectomy (only curative option)
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Immunotherapy (IVIG, steroids, tacrolimus,
rituximab) slows progression

name: FIRES (Febrile Infection- Related Epilepsy Syndrome)
description: Life-threatening new-onset refractory status epilepticus following a febrile illness; leads to severe epilepsy and cognitive impairment.

frequency.sources: FIRES: ~1/1,000,000 children annually. Consistent with published case series. Atlas confirmed.

diagnosis: Clinical (febrile illness → super- refractory status epilepticus); EEG; MRI (late T2 changes); IL-6, IL-1β elevated; CSF studies

treatment.standardOfCare:
Anesthesia for status epilepticus; high-dose steroids;
IVIG; ketogenic diet
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Anakinra (IL-1 inhibitor) emerging evidence;
rituximab

name: Landau-Kleffner Syndrome
description: Acquired epileptic aphasia in children; progressive language regression with epileptiform EEG activity during sleep.

frequency.sources: Landau-Kleffner: ~200 cases reported annually worldwide; atlas confirmed. Rare; prevalence not formally established.

diagnosis: EEG (bilateral temporal spike-waves, markedly worse in sleep); language regression; CSWS pattern; rule out structural lesion

treatment.standardOfCare: Valproate, clobazam, ACTH; speech therapy; benzodiazepines for CSWS
treatment.emerging: Emerging: Subpial transection in refractory cases; language rehab trials

name: CSWS / Electrical Status Epilepticus in Sleep (ESES)
description: EEG pattern of near-continuous spike-wave during slow-wave sleep causing cognitive regression and behavioral changes.

frequency.sources: CSWS/ESES: ~0.2–0.5% of children with epilepsy. Atlas confirmed. No population-based prevalence established separately from epilepsy prevalence.

diagnosis: Sleep EEG (continuous spike-wave >85% NREM); neuropsychological testing; MRI; identify underlying etiology

treatment.standardOfCare:
Valproate, clobazam, ethosuximide, ACTH; diazepam
overnight; speech/cognitive therapy
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Sulthiame (Europe, off-label); EEG-guided therapy
optimization

name: GLUT1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glucose Transporter Type 1)
description: Deficiency of glucose transport across blood-brain barrier causing epilepsy, intellectual disability, and movement disorder; responds to ketogenic diet.

frequency.global: ~60,000 – ~80,000 ✓ VERIFIED [UPDATED]: Orphanet: prevalence 1/25,000–1/80,000 (broader than atlas). Atlas states 1/90,000– 100,000 which is at the rarer end of Orphanet's range. Recommend updating to 1/25,000–1/80,000 per Orphanet. Likely underdiagnosed.

diagnosis: Low CSF glucose (<40 mg/dL) with normal blood glucose; CSF:blood glucose ratio <0.45; SLC2A1 gene sequencing

treatment.standardOfCare:
Ketogenic diet (first-line, highly effective); modified
Atkins diet
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Avoid glucose-lowering drugs and fasting;
triheptanoin investigational

name: Pyridoxine-Dependent Epilepsy
description: Autosomal recessive disorder with neonatal/infantile seizures fully responsive to high-dose pyridoxine; caused by ALDH7A1 mutations.

frequency.sources: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy: 1/400,000–700,000. Orphanet confirms very rare; consistent with atlas.

diagnosis: ALDH7A1 gene sequencing; pyridoxine trial (IV); elevated pipecolic acid / alpha- AASA in urine/plasma; CSF neurotransmitters

treatment.standardOfCare:
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation (lifelong);
folinic acid adjunct
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Lysine-restricted diet; alpha-aminoadipic
semialdehyde biomarker-guided titration

name: Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsy — Unverricht- Lundborg
description: Autosomal recessive PME with action myoclonus, tonic-clonic seizures, and progressive ataxia; onset ages 6–15.

frequency.sources: Unverricht-Lundborg: ~1/20,000 in Finland; rarer globally. Atlas confirmed. Orphanet: prevalence 1– 9/100,000 in Finland; much rarer elsewhere.

diagnosis: CSTB gene sequencing; EEG giant SEP; clinical (progressive myoclonus + ataxia, onset 6–15yr); brain MRI (cerebellar atrophy late)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Valproate, clonazepam, levetiracetam, piracetam; avoid
phenytoin
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy; gene therapy
preclinical

name: Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsy — Lafora Disease
description: Autosomal recessive PME with rapid neurological deterioration; caused by EPM2A/NHLRC1 mutations; typically fatal within 10 years.

frequency.sources: Lafora disease: ~1/500,000 globally; most common PME in South Asia. Atlas confirmed. Orphanet: prevalence <1/1,000,000.

diagnosis: EPM2A/NHLRC1 gene sequencing; skin biopsy Lafora bodies (periodic acid-Schiff stain); EEG; clinical (adolescent onset rapid decline)

treatment.standardOfCare: Valproate, clonazepam, levetiracetam
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Metformin (targets glycogen synthesis,
investigational); no approved disease-modifying therapy

name: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex — Epilepsy
description: Multi-system genetic disorder (TSC1/TSC2) with cortical tubers causing epilepsy in ~90% of patients, often drug-resistant.

frequency.sources: TSC overall: Orphanet ~1/6,000–10,000. Atlas notes ~8– 12/100K with epilepsy in ~90%. Consistent with Orphanet's prevalence when epilepsy subset calculated. Atlas confirmed.

diagnosis: TSC1/TSC2 gene sequencing; MRI (tubers, SEN, SEGA); EEG; ophthalmology; renal ultrasound

treatment.standardOfCare:
Vigabatrin (infantile spasms); everolimus (Afinitor) FDA
for SEGA + seizures; epilepsy surgery
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Cannabidiol (Epidiolex) FDA 2020; mTOR inhibitor
optimization trials. Radiprodil (GluN2B NAM) — Astroscape
Study (NCT06392009) actively enrolling (GRIN Therapeutics);
targets GluN2B overexpression in TSC brain tissue,
addressing seizure mechanism distinct from mTOR pathway

name: Absence Epilepsy — Childhood & Juvenile Onset (CAE / JAE)
description: Common idiopathic generalized epilepsy with brief staring spells (absence seizures); CAE onset 4–8 years, JAE 8–12 years.

frequency.sources: CAE ~6–8/100K, JAE ~1– 2/100K. Consistent with published literature (ILAE, Orphanet). Atlas confirmed.

diagnosis: EEG (3Hz generalized spike-wave, provoked by hyperventilation); clinical; exclude other causes of staring

treatment.standardOfCare:
Ethosuximide (first-line CAE); valproate (first-line JAE);
lamotrigine
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: 65–70% remission by adulthood; CGRP pathway
research

name: Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME)
description: Common idiopathic generalized epilepsy with early-morning myoclonic jerks, tonic-clonic seizures, and absences; onset adolescence.

frequency.sources: JME: ~5–10% of all epilepsies; 5–10/100K adolescents. Atlas confirmed. Widely cited figures in epilepsy literature.

diagnosis: EEG (4–6Hz generalized polyspike- wave, photosensitivity); morning myoclonus + GTCS; clinical diagnosis + EEG

treatment.standardOfCare:
Valproate (most effective); lamotrigine, levetiracetam;
lifelong treatment required
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: 90%+ seizure control achievable; perampanel
adjunct trials

name: Febrile Seizures & Febrile Seizures Plus (GEFS+)
description: Most common seizure disorder in children; provoked by fever; GEFS+ is a genetic spectrum with febrile and afebrile seizures.

frequency.sources: Febrile seizures: 2–5% of children ages 6 mo–5 yr. Atlas confirmed. CDC and AAP cite this range.

diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; EEG only if complex features; gene panel (SCN1A, SCN1B, GABRG2) for GEFS+

treatment.standardOfCare:
Acute: rectal diazepam / intranasal midazolam;
prophylaxis rarely needed
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: GEFS+ spectrum: individualized genetic treatment
approaches

name: Focal Cortical Dysplasia (FCD — Types I, II, III)
description: Malformation of cortical development causing focal drug-resistant epilepsy; most common cause of epilepsy surgery in children.
diagnosis: High-resolution 3T MRI (FCD protocol); FDG-PET; MEG; SEEG/EEG for localization; somatic variant testing (mTOR pathway) on surgical tissue

treatment.standardOfCare:
Resective epilepsy surgery (curative if complete
resection)
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: mTOR inhibitors investigational; radiosurgery; LITT
for deep FCD. Radiprodil (GluN2B NAM) — Astroscape Study
(NCT06392009) actively enrolling (GRIN Therapeutics); targets increased GluN2B subunit expression driving seizure
activity in dysplastic cortex

name: KCNT1-Related Epilepsies (MMFSI / ADNFLE)
description: Severe gain-of-function channelopathy causing malignant migrating focal seizures of infancy (MMFSI) or nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy.

frequency.global: ~200 – ~300 Insufficent Data : Estimates based on: KCNT1 epilepsies: very rare (<300 cases globally). Atlas confirmed. No population prevalence established.

diagnosis: KCNT1 gene sequencing; EEG; neonatal/infancy-onset migrating focal seizures (MMFSI) or ADNFLE pattern

treatment.standardOfCare: Standard ASMs (limited efficacy)
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Quinidine (gain-of-function blocker, variable
response); no FDA approval; clinical trials ongoing

name: DEPDC5-Related Focal Epilepsies
description: Autosomal dominant focal epilepsy caused by DEPDC5 mutations in the mTOR pathway; variable severity, sometimes with SUDEP risk.

frequency.sources: DEPDC5: ~1% of familial focal epilepsies. Atlas confirmed. No population prevalence figure available; familial fraction estimate consistent with published studies.

diagnosis: DEPDC5 sequencing; brain MRI (may be normal or show subtle FCD); family history; SEEG for surgical planning

treatment.standardOfCare: Standard ASMs; resective surgery if lesion identified
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin/everolimus)
investigational

name: STXBP1-Related Disorders (Ohtahara / West overlap)
description: STXBP1 mutations causing early epileptic encephalopathy, intellectual disability, and movement disorder; one of most common DEE genes.

frequency.sources: STXBP1: ~1/100,000. Atlas confirmed. Consistently cited as one of most common single-gene DEE causes; ~1–2% of all epileptic encephalopathies.

diagnosis: STXBP1 gene sequencing; EEG; neonatal/infantile onset; clinical spectrum from Ohtahara to West to unclassified DEE

treatment.standardOfCare: Phenobarbital, ACTH, vigabatrin; ketogenic diet
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy; avoid levetiracetam
(may worsen); gene therapy preclinical

name: SLC6A1-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder
description: Myoclonic-atonic epilepsy and intellectual disability caused by SLC6A1 (GAT-1) mutations; typically de novo.

frequency.sources: SLC6A1: ~1/50,000– 100,000 with WES. Atlas confirmed. Increasingly recognized with expanded genetic testing.

diagnosis: SLC6A1 gene sequencing; EEG (myoclonic-atonic); MAE phenotype; intellectual disability

treatment.standardOfCare: Valproate, ethosuximide; ketogenic diet
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: OV101 (gaboxadol) trials completed, not FDA
approved; no targeted therapy

name: Developmental & Epileptic Encephalopathies (DEE — umbrella)
description: Umbrella term for severe epilepsies where both seizures and underlying etiology contribute to developmental impairment.

frequency.sources: DEE umbrella: collective ~1–2/1,000 children. Atlas confirmed. Broad category encompassing many genetic and structural causes.

diagnosis: Comprehensive epilepsy gene panel (300+ genes); EEG; MRI; metabolic workup; chromosomal microarray

treatment.standardOfCare:
Gene-specific ASM therapy; ketogenic diet; VNS; IVIG in
autoimmune forms
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Precision DEE gene therapy programs; digital
biomarker trials

name: Hypothalamic Hamartoma — Gelastic Epilepsy
description: Benign brain lesion causing gelastic (laughing) seizures, precocious puberty, and behavioral problems; seizures often drug-resistant.

frequency.sources: Hypothalamic hamartoma/gelastic epilepsy: ~1/200,000 children. US urban study: 1/225,000. Atlas confirmed.

diagnosis: MRI (sessile or pedunculated HH); EEG (frontal/bifrontal); clinical (gelastic/dacrystic seizures, precocious puberty)

treatment.standardOfCare: Radiosurgery (Gamma Knife); transcallosal resection
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT); MRI-guided
focused ultrasound

name: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
description: Neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviors; wide phenotypic spectrum.

frequency.global: ~51.0M – ~76.5M ✓ VERIFIED [UPDATED]: CDC ADDM Network 2022 (MMWR Apr 2025): 1 in 36 (2.8%) 8-yr-olds identified with ASD — up from 1 in 44 (2023 report). Atlas estimate of 1–2% likely based on older data; current US prevalence is ~2.8%. Global WHO estimate remains ~1% but rising with improved detection. Recommend updating atlas to reflect 1 in 36 US figure.
frequency.sources: Shaw et al., MMWR 74(2), April 2025.

diagnosis: DSM-5 behavioral criteria; ADOS-2 + ADI-R gold standard; developmental screening (M-CHAT); genetic workup (chromosomal microarray, fragile X, MECP2)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Aripiprazole + risperidone (FDA for irritability); intensive
behavioral therapy (ABA); speech, OT
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No FDA-approved disease-modifying therapy;
oxytocin, SHANK3 ASOs in trials

name: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
description: Neurodevelopmental disorder with persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity impairing daily functioning.

frequency.us: children ages 3–17; most prevalent pediatric neuro condition US: ~6.0M – ~7.5M
frequency.global: ~180M – ~230M ✓ VERIFIED [UPDATED]: CDC/NSCH 2022 (Danielson et al., J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol 2024): 7.1 million (11.4%) US children ages 3–17 ever diagnosed with ADHD. NCHS Data Brief 499 (March 2024): 11.3% ages 5–17. Atlas estimate of 9–10% is below the current 11.3–11.4% official figure. Recommend updating to ~11% US. Global estimate ~5–7% (Polanczyk et al.).
frequency.sources: CDC NCHS, NSCH 2022.

diagnosis: DSM-5 clinical criteria; rating scales (Vanderbilt, Conners); rule out sleep disorders, anxiety, learning disabilities; no biomarker

treatment.standardOfCare:
Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine salts) FDA
approved; behavioral therapy
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Viloxazine (Qelbree) FDA 2021; non-stimulants
(atomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine)

name: Rett Syndrome (MECP2)
description: X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder almost exclusively in females; developmental regression, loss of purposeful hand use, breathing irregularities.

frequency.sources: Rett syndrome (MECP2): 1/10,000–1/15,000 females. Orphanet confirms prevalence 1–9/100,000 females. NORD: ~1/10,000–15,000 people (predominantly females). Atlas confirmed. Males with MECP2 duplication represent a separate, severe presentation.

diagnosis: MECP2 gene sequencing; clinical criteria (Hagberg criteria); rule out other causes of regression

treatment.standardOfCare:
Trofinetide (Daybue) FDA 2023 — first approved
therapy; symptomatic (seizure, scoliosis, GI, cardiac)
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: MECP2 gene therapy (AAV9 trials); IGF-1 pathway
agents

name: FOXG1 Syndrome
description: Severe congenital variant of Rett syndrome with earlier onset, absence of normal development, and hyperkinetic movements; caused by FOXG1 mutations.

frequency.sources: FOXG1 syndrome: Orphanet reports prevalence <1/1,000,000. Estimated <1,000 cases globally. Atlas rate confirmed as very rare. Recognition rapidly increasing with WES availability.

diagnosis: FOXG1 gene sequencing; MRI (simplified gyral pattern, hypoplastic corpus callosum); clinical (congenital variant Rett-like)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Symptomatic management; supportive multidisciplinary
care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Clinical trials exploring IGF-1 pathway; no approved
therapy

name: Angelman Syndrome
description: Neurodevelopmental syndrome with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, happy demeanor, and seizures; caused by maternal UBE3A loss.

frequency.sources: Angelman syndrome: ~1/12,000–15,000 live births per Orphanet and published epidemiological studies (Petersen et al.; Danish cohort). Atlas confirmed. ~500–600 new US cases/yr.

diagnosis: DNA methylation analysis (chromosome 15q11-q13); UBE3A sequencing; EEG (characteristic high-amplitude delta); FISH for deletion

treatment.standardOfCare:
Seizure management (valproate, clonazepam);
supportive behavioral care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: ASO therapy (UBE3A unsilencing) in Phase 2/3
trials; gene replacement

name: Pitt-Hopkins Syndrome
description: TCF4 haploinsufficiency causing intellectual disability, absent/limited speech, breathing anomalies, and distinctive facial features.

frequency.sources: Pitt-Hopkins syndrome (TCF4): Orphanet prevalence <1/100,000. Estimated 1/34,000–41,000 births in European studies. Atlas confirmed. Increasingly identified with WES.

diagnosis: TCF4 gene sequencing; clinical (intellectual disability, breathing irregularities, distinctive facies)

treatment.standardOfCare: Symptomatic supportive care; breathing management
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Clinical trials targeting TCF4 pathway; no approved
therapy

name: Fragile X Syndrome
description: Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability; caused by FMR1 CGG repeat expansion; associated with autism and behavioral challenges.

frequency.global: ~500,000 – ~700,000 ✓ VERIFIED [UPDATED]: Fragile X syndrome: Most current literature (PMC 2025 systematic review; CDC stakeholder report) cites 1/4,000–5,000 males and 1/6,000–8,000 females. Combined prevalence ~1/5,000–7,000 males and 1/4,000–6,000 females. Some atlas versions state 1/4,000 males — this is at the higher end but defensible. The 'fragile X prevalence paradox' paper (PMC) suggests true prevalence may be ~1/2,500 (all sexes) when including

diagnosis: FMR1 CGG repeat expansion (PCR + Southern blot); methylation analysis; FMRP protein level

treatment.standardOfCare: Symptomatic (stimulants, SSRIs, antipsychotics)
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy; metformin,
minocycline, mGluR5 antagonists — trials failed

name: Prader-Willi Syndrome
description: Complex neurodevelopmental disorder with hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability, and behavioral problems; chromosome 15q11-q13 abnormality.

frequency.sources: Prader-Willi syndrome: Orphanet ~1/10,000–30,000. Most population studies converge on 1/10,000–25,000. NORD: 1/10,000– 20,000. Atlas confirmed.

diagnosis: DNA methylation (chromosome 15q11- q13); FISH; UPD analysis; clinical criteria

treatment.standardOfCare:
Growth hormone (FDA approved); strict caloric
restriction
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: GLP-1 agonists investigational; carbetocin for
hyperphagia trials

name: Williams Syndrome
description: Deletion of chromosome 7q11.23 causing intellectual disability, hypersociability, cardiovascular disease, and characteristic facial features.

frequency.sources: Williams syndrome: Population studies (Strømme et al., J Child Neurol 2002): ~1/7,500. Orphanet: 1/7,500–20,000. Atlas confirmed. ~30,000 individuals in US estimated by Williams Syndrome Association.

diagnosis: FISH or chromosomal microarray (7q11.23 deletion); clinical (elfin facies, hypercalcemia, supravalvular AS)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Cardiac surgery for SVAS; calcium restriction; early
intervention, speech therapy
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy; ELN gene therapy
preclinical

name: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome (DiGeorge / Velocardiofacial)
description: Most common chromosomal microdeletion syndrome; causes CHD, immune deficiency, learning disabilities, and high schizophrenia risk.

frequency.sources: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/VCF): 1/2,000–4,000 live births per Orphanet. Most cited figure is ~1/4,000. Atlas confirmed. Most common chromosomal microdeletion syndrome.

diagnosis: Chromosomal microarray (MLPA or SNP array); FISH for classic deletion; clinical screening

treatment.standardOfCare:
Cardiac surgery; calcium supplementation;
immunoglobulin for immune deficiency
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy; psychiatric
monitoring protocols

name: Cornelia de Lange Syndrome
description: Multisystem developmental disorder with intellectual disability, growth restriction, limb anomalies, and behavioral challenges; NIPBL and other genes.

frequency.sources: Cornelia de Lange syndrome: Orphanet ~1/10,000–30,000. NORD: ~1/10,000. Atlas confirmed. Likely underdiagnosed; estimated ~30,000–40,000 in US.

diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; gene panel (NIPBL, SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21, HDAC8); chromosomal microarray

treatment.standardOfCare:
Multidisciplinary: cardiac, GI, orthopedic, behavioral;
early intervention
treatment.emerging:

diagnosis: Urine S-sulfocysteine, xanthine, uric acid; MOCS1/2/3 or GPHN sequencing; molybdopterin cofactor assay

treatment.standardOfCare:
cPMP replacement (fosdenopterin/NULIBRY) FDA 2021
for Type A
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Types B/C: no approved therapy; gene therapy
preclinical

name: TBCK-Related Encephalopathy (TBCK Syndrome)
description: TBCK mutations causing hypotonia, intellectual disability, progressive brain atrophy, and seizures; enriched in Hispanic populations.

frequency.global: ~50 – ~100 Insufficent Data : Estimates based on: TBCK-Related Encephalopathy (TBCK Syndrome): Orphanet prevalence unknown / <1/1,000,000. Described in 2015; ~70 cases globally as of 2024. No population prevalence established. Atlas estimate is best current approximation. Likely underdiagnosed pre-WES era.
frequency.sources: Bharat et al. Am J Hum Genet 2016; NORD; Orphanet.

diagnosis: TBCK gene sequencing; MRI (progressive brain atrophy); clinical (severe ID, hypotonia, epilepsy)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Supportive care; seizure management; ~100 known
patients
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: mTOR pathway research ongoing; no approved
therapy

name: Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome (AGS)
description: Interferonopathy caused by mutations in RNASEH2A/B/C, TREX1, SAMHD1, ADAR, or IFIH1; causes progressive encephalopathy, intracranial calcifications, and CSF lymphocytosis; JAK inhibitor trials ongoing.
diagnosis: Gene panel (RNASEH2A/B/C, TREX1, SAMHD1, ADAR, IFIH1); CSF IFN-α; brain MRI (calcifications); interferon signature (ISG15 score)

treatment.standardOfCare: Supportive care; seizure management
treatment.emerging: Emerging: No FDA-approved therapy; JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, ruxolitinib) in clinical trials; reverse transcriptase inhibitors investigational

name: Vanishing White Matter Disease (VWM / CACH)
description: EIF2B mutations causing progressive white matter loss triggered by febrile illness or minor head trauma; episodic neurological deterioration.

frequency.sources: Vanishing White Matter Disease (VWM/CACH): Orphanet prevalence <1/100,000. ~500+ cases in global literature. EIF2B1–5 gene variants causative. Most common in children; stress-triggered acute neurological deterioration characteristic. Atlas confirmed. No approved treatment. Source: Orphanet; GeneReviews NBK1451; NORD.

diagnosis: EIF2B1-5 gene sequencing; MRI (diffuse white matter signal change, fluid-like white matter); CSF normal; clinical trigger history

treatment.standardOfCare: Avoid fever/head trauma triggers; supportive care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No approved disease-modifying therapy;
fosigotifator (eIF2B activator) Phase 2

name: Cerebrotendinous Xanthomatosis (CTX)
description: CYP27A1 sterol metabolism defect causing progressive neurological disease, tendon xanthomas, cataracts, and premature atherosclerosis; treatable with chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA).

frequency.sources: Cerebrotendinous Xanthomatosis (CTX): Orphanet prevalence 1/50,000–1/100,000. ~300– 500 US cases historically estimated; likely underdiagnosed pre-NBS era. Added to RUSP 2020; NBS expanding. Atlas confirmed. Chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) highly effective — diagnosis-to- treatment urgency critical. Source: Orphanet; GeneReviews NBK1409; NORD.

diagnosis: CYP27A1 gene sequencing; plasma cholestanol (elevated); urine bile alcohols; serum 7α- hydroxycholestenone; brain MRI

treatment.standardOfCare:
Chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) highly effective (FDA-
designated); ezetimibe adjunct; statins
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Treat early before irreversible damage; newborn
screening programs

name: 4H Syndrome / POLR3- Related Leukodystrophy
description: Biallelic POLR3A/POLR3B mutations causing hypomyelination, hypodontia, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia.

frequency.sources: 4H Syndrome / POLR3- Related Leukodystrophy: Orphanet prevalence <1/1,000,000. ~100–150 cases globally. POLR3A/B/C variants causative. Hypomyelination + hypodontia + hypogonadism triad. Atlas confirmed. Orphanet notes insufficient data for precise prevalence. Source: Orphanet; Bernard G. Semin Pediatr Neurol 2016; NORD.

diagnosis: POLR3A/POLR3B gene sequencing; MRI (hypomyelination + cerebellar atrophy); dentition X-ray (hypodontia); endocrine workup

treatment.standardOfCare:
Symptomatic (growth hormone, dental care,
physiotherapy)
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No approved therapy; CHOP Global
Leukodystrophy Registry studies

name: Zellweger Spectrum Disorder (PEX mutations)
description: Peroxisome biogenesis disorders (PEX1–PEX26) causing progressive neurological decline, retinal dystrophy, hearing loss, and liver disease; Zellweger syndrome is the most severe form.

frequency.sources: Zellweger Spectrum Disorder (PEX mutations): Orphanet prevalence ~1/50,000; birth incidence ~1/25,000–1/50,000 (all PBD-ZSD spectrum). Classic Zellweger most severe; neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy and infantile Refsum milder. Atlas confirmed. On US NBS panel for X-ALD (peroxisomal panel adds detection). Source: Orphanet; GeneReviews NBK1448; NORD.

diagnosis: PEX gene panel (PEX1 most common); plasma VLCFA elevated; bile acid intermediates; plasmalogens (decreased); peroxisome biogenesis assay

treatment.standardOfCare:
DHA supplementation; bile acid (CDCA, cholic acid);
dietary fat modification
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy for severe forms;
AAV-PEX gene therapy preclinical

name: Cockayne Syndrome
description: ERCC6/ERCC8 DNA repair deficiency causing progressive neurodegeneration, photosensitivity, growth failure, and premature aging; no disease-modifying therapy approved.

frequency.sources: Cockayne Syndrome: Orphanet prevalence ~1/200,000– 1/500,000. ~200 cases reported in US. CSA (ERCC8) and CSB (ERCC6) variants causative — nucleotide excision repair defect. Atlas confirmed. No specific treatment; sun avoidance and supportive care. Source: Orphanet; GeneReviews NBK1342; NORD.

diagnosis: ERCC6/ERCC8 gene sequencing; UV sensitivity testing (fibroblasts); clinical criteria (microcephaly, sun sensitivity, cataracts, short stature, neurodegeneration)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Sun avoidance; symptomatic management; nutritional
support; hearing aids
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No approved disease-modifying therapy; DNA
repair pathway research

name: Multiple Sulfatase Deficiency (MSD)
description: SUMF1 mutations causing combined deficiency of all sulfatases; features of multiple MPS types plus ichthyosis and severe neurological decline.

frequency.sources: Multiple Sulfatase Deficiency (MSD): Orphanet prevalence <1/1,000,000. ~100 cases globally as of 2023. SUMF1 gene — deficiency of all sulfatases combined. Atlas confirmed. No approved therapy; HSCT palliative. Source: Orphanet; Schlotawa L. J Inherit Metab Dis 2011; NORD.

diagnosis: SUMF1 gene sequencing; multiple sulfatase enzyme activities (all deficient); urine GAGs + sulfatides; MRI

treatment.standardOfCare:
Supportive care; ERTs not effective due to SUMF1
defect
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No approved therapy; SUMF1 enzyme replacement
research

name: Sjogren-Larsson Syndrome
description: ALDH3A2 fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency causing ichthyosis, intellectual disability, spastic diplegia, and macular degeneration.
diagnosis: ALDH3A2 gene sequencing; leukotriene B4 elevated; skin biopsy (lipid lamellar bodies); clinical triad

treatment.standardOfCare:
Dietary fat modification; symptomatic spasticity
management
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Zileuton (5-LOX inhibitor, off-label) reduces LTB4
levels; no FDA approval

name: Megalencephalic Leukoencephalopathy with Subcortical Cysts (MLC)
description: MLC1 or GLIALCAM mutations causing macrocephaly, slowly progressive ataxia, and subcortical cysts on MRI; distinct from MLC2 (remitting form).

frequency.sources: Megalencephalic Leukoencephalopathy with Subcortical Cysts (MLC): Orphanet prevalence <1/1,000,000. ~150 cases globally. MLC1 (80%) and GLIALCAM/HEPACAM (20%) variants. Highly prevalent in specific founder populations (Agarwal community in India). Atlas confirmed. No specific treatment; mild and slow- progressing in most. Source: Orphanet; van der Knaap MS. GeneReviews NBK1535; NORD.

diagnosis: MLC1/GLIALCAM gene sequencing; MRI (macrocephaly + diffuse white matter signal + subcortical cysts anterior temporal); clinical

treatment.standardOfCare: Seizure management; physiotherapy; supportive care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No approved therapy; MLC2 (GLIALCAM-related)
may remit spontaneously

name: Nonketotic Hyperglycinemia (NKH / Glycine Encephalopathy)
description: GLDC/AMT/GCSH deficiency causing glycine accumulation in CSF and plasma; classic neonatal form presents with severe encephalopathy, hypotonia, myoclonic seizures, apnea, and hiccups; atypical form causes spastic diplegia and cognitive decline.

frequency.global: ~52,000 – ~67,000 global cases Orphanet: 1/76,000; NORD: 1/60,000– 76,000; higher in Finnish (~1/12,000) and Bedouin Israeli (~1/5,000) populations. GLDC mutations ~80%; AMT ~15%; GCSH <1%. Classic neonatal form most severe; atypical forms include late-onset spastic diplegia and spinocerebellar degeneration variant.

diagnosis: Plasma and CSF glycine (CSF:plasma ratio >0.08 diagnostic); GLDC/AMT/GCSH gene panel; EEG (burst suppression in neonates; hypsarrhythmia may develop); MRI brain (thin/absent corpus callosum, delayed myelination, periventricular diffusion restriction); urine organic acids (rule out ketotic hyperglycinemias)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Sodium benzoate (lowers plasma glycine; 250–750
mg/kg/day); dextromethorphan or ketamine (NMDA receptor
antagonists to reduce excitotoxic glycine neurotoxicity);
antiseizure medications; NOTE: valproate AVOIDED — raises
glycine levels
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: High-dose dextromethorphan protocols (glycinergic
NMDA receptor blockade); biomarker-guided dosing (CSF
glycine monitoring); dietary glycine/serine manipulation; gene
therapy preclinical (AAV-GLDC mouse models); glycine
cleavage system enzyme replacement research; sodium
benzoate slow-release formulation trials

name: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) — Neonatal
description: Brain injury from perinatal oxygen deprivation; leading cause of neonatal death and neurodevelopmental disability; hypothermia is standard of care.

frequency.global: ~2.3M – ~6.9M US: ~6,100 – ~10,800 new cases/yr | Global: ~840,000 – ~1,400,000 new cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — Cornet et al. Pediatric Neurology 2023; US incidence 1–3/1,000 live births (1.7/1,000 in KPNC study); global ~1.5–3/1,000 in high-income countries, up to 26/1,000 in LMICs; standard of care: therapeutic hypothermia within 6 hrs for moderate- severe HIE

diagnosis: Thompson score (clinical); amplitude- integrated EEG (aEEG); conventional EEG; MRI at day 4–7 (DWI + MRS); cord gas (pH, base deficit)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Therapeutic hypothermia (33.5°C ×72h) — standard of
care for moderate-severe HIE
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Erythropoietin + melatonin adjuncts in trials;
umbilical cord blood stem cells Phase 2

name: Periventricular Leukomalacia (PVL) — Prematurity-Related
description: White matter injury in premature neonates from ischemia and inflammation; leading cause of cerebral palsy in premature infants.

frequency.global: ~120,000 – ~160,000 US: ~7,000 – ~14,000 prevalent US pediatric cases | Global: ~220,000 – ~440,000 prevalent global cases ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — Neonatal radiological review PMC 2017; affects ~25–50% of VLBW premature infants (<1,500g, ~28,000 US/yr); majority minor; cystic PVL (severe) ~5–10% of VLBW; cumulative pediatric cases estimated from preterm birth rates

diagnosis: Cranial ultrasound (serial, bedside); MRI at term-equivalent age; clinical neurological exam; neurodevelopmental follow-up

treatment.standardOfCare:
Antenatal steroids + MgSO4 neuroprotection
(prevention); early EI/therapy
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Erythropoietin trials post-injury; no specific
pharmacotherapy proven

name: Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH) — Neonatal
description: Bleeding into the germinal matrix/ventricles in premature infants; grades III-IV associated with long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

frequency.global: ~200,000 – ~375,000 US: ~6,300 – ~8,400 new US cases/yr | Global: ~245,000 – ~330,000 new global cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — VLBW births ~28,000/yr US; Grade III-IV IVH ~22–30% of VLBW; all grades IVH up to 45% in <28 wks; globally ~3.5M VLBW births/yr; significant neurological morbidity in grades III–IV

diagnosis: Serial cranial ultrasound (Papile grading I–IV); head circumference; lumbar puncture for hemorrhagic hydrocephalus

treatment.standardOfCare:
VP shunt/reservoir for post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus;
indomethacin prophylaxis for IVH prevention
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No pharmacotherapy of proven benefit post-IVH;
DRIFT procedure investigational

name: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) — Pediatric
description: Leading cause of death and acquired disability in children; includes concussion to severe TBI from falls, MVA, and abusive head trauma.

frequency.global: ~11.3M – ~20.9M US: ~2.2M – ~3.8M ED visits/yr (all ages); ~400,000 – ~600,000 moderate- severe cases/yr | Global: ~27,000,000 – ~69,000,000 all-severity cases/yr globally ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — CDC TBI data; ~1.5M children seen for TBI annually US; ~400,000–600,000 moderate-severe; leading cause of disability and death ages 1–44; includes concussion (mild TBI) as predominant subtype

diagnosis: CT head (acute); MRI (subacute/chronic); GCS scoring; ICP monitoring if severe; PET/DTI for research

treatment.standardOfCare:
Mild: rest + gradual return to activity; Moderate-severe:
ICP management, surgery; rehabilitation
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No neuroprotective agent approved; progesterone,
amantadine trials

name: Acute Flaccid Myelitis (AFM — post-enteroviral)
description: Acute spinal cord inflammation causing rapid limb weakness; predominantly affects children; linked to enterovirus D68.

frequency.global: ~2,300 – ~6,900 US: ~28 – ~120 confirmed cases/yr (non- epidemic); ~240 in peak epidemic years (2018) | Global: ~500 – ~2,000 cases/yr globally (estimated; surveillance incomplete)

diagnosis: MRI spine (T2 gray matter lesion anterior horn); CSF pleocytosis; nasopharyngeal/rectal swab (EV-D68, EV-A71); NCS/EMG

treatment.standardOfCare:
Intensive neurorehabilitation; ventilatory support;
supportive care
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No FDA-approved specific therapy; IVIG (limited
evidence); fluoxetine investigational

name: Pediatric Arterial Ischemic Stroke
description: Stroke from arterial occlusion in children beyond the neonatal period; causes include cardiac, arteriopathy, thrombophilia, and sickle cell.

frequency.global: ~46,000 – ~300,000 US: ~1,100 – ~5,800 new cases/yr | Global: ~44,000 – ~230,000 new cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — AHA Scientific Statement 2019 (Ferriero et al.); childhood AIS incidence 1.2– 7.9/100,000/yr; highest rates in Black children and infants <1 yr; leading childhood stroke subtype; ~55% of pediatric strokes are ischemic

diagnosis: MRI brain + DWI; MRA head/neck; echocardiogram; thrombophilia panel; CBC; inflammatory markers; lumbar puncture if indicated

treatment.standardOfCare:
Antiplatelet (aspirin) or anticoagulation per etiology;
rehabilitation
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: tPA (limited pediatric data, case-by-case); PASTA
trial (steroids for FCA)

name: Perinatal Stroke
description: Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke occurring from 20 weeks gestation through 28 days of life; common cause of hemiplegia and epilepsy.

frequency.global: ~28,000 – ~61,000 US: ~2,200 – ~7,200 new US cases/yr | Global: ~35,000 – ~117,000 new global cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — Perinatal stroke incidence 1:1,100–5,000 live births (US ~0.6–3.3/1,000); PMC review 2023; includes PAIS and presumed perinatal stroke; neonates have highest stroke risk ratio; MCA territory most common; often presents delayed (weeks to months post- birth)

diagnosis: MRI brain + DWI; echocardiogram; thrombophilia panel; placental pathology; EEG (seizure monitoring)

treatment.standardOfCare:
Seizure management (phenobarbital); constraint-

treatment.emerging:
Emerging: No acute thrombolysis in neonates; early-
intervention plasticity protocols

name: Cerebral Sinovenous Thrombosis (CSVT)
description: Thrombosis of dural venous sinuses causing elevated ICP, seizures, and focal deficits; neonates and adolescents at highest risk.

frequency.global: ~11,000 – ~20,000 US: ~500 – ~1,450 new US cases/yr (all ages); ~250–750/yr pediatric | Global: ~20,000 – ~60,000 new global cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — AHA 2019 Statement; CSVT incidence 0.67/100,000 children/yr; neonatal CSVT 2.6–12/100,000 term infants/yr; presents with headache, seizures, focal deficits; anticoagulation is standard treatment

diagnosis: MRI with MRV; CT venography if MRI unavailable; thrombophilia panel; CBC; LP for ICP

treatment.standardOfCare:
Anticoagulation (LMWH then warfarin, 3–6 months);

treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Thrombolysis for deterioration; treat underlying
cause

name: Hemorrhagic Stroke — Pediatric
description: Intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage in children; causes include AVM, coagulopathy, and hypertension.

frequency.global: ~25,000 – ~53,000 US: ~730 – ~1,240 new US pediatric cases/yr | Global: ~29,000 – ~50,000 new global cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — AHA 2019 Statement; hemorrhagic stroke ~50% of pediatric stroke; incidence 1– 1.7/100,000 children/yr; higher mortality than ischemic (up to 25%); AVM is leading cause in children >1 yr

diagnosis: CT head (acute); MRI/MRA/MRV; conventional angiography for vascular malformation; coagulation panel

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical evacuation if life-threatening; endovascular
treatment for AVM/aneurysm; rehabilitation
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Reverse anticoagulation; minimally invasive
evacuation techniques

name: Moyamoya Disease / Syndrome
description: Progressive occlusion of internal carotid arteries with collateral 'puff of smoke' vessels; causes ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke.

frequency.global: ~1,600 – ~3,000 US: ~1,100 – ~3,300 total US pediatric cases | Global: ~22,000 – ~66,000 total global pediatric cases ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — Practical Neurology review 2024; US incidence 0.086/100,000; most common cerebrovascular disease in children in Japan (~3/100,000 children); bimodal distribution: age ~5 and 30–40 yrs; RNF213 susceptibility gene in East Asians; surgical revascularization reduces stroke risk

diagnosis: MRI/MRA (progressive stenosis ICA/proximal MCA/ACA, collateral 'puff of smoke'); conventional angiography for surgical planning

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical revascularization (STA-MCA bypass, EDAS,
pial synangiosis) — standard of care; aspirin
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Calcium channel blockers; no pharmacological
cure; stem cell adjunct trials

name: Cerebral Cavernous Malformations (CCM)
description: Clusters of abnormal blood vessels prone to hemorrhage causing seizures, focal deficits, and headache.

frequency.global: ~2.3M – ~11.5M US: ~2,100 – ~5,100 US pediatric symptomatic cases | Global: ~84,000 – ~200,000 global cases ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — GeneReviews CCM; prevalence ~1/200 individuals but most asymptomatic; symptomatic CCM ~1/625 (0.16–0.5%); sporadic or familial (CCM1-KRIT1, CCM2, CCM3-PDCD10); hemorrhage risk ~0.5–3%/yr; MRI with gradient echo sequence for diagnosis

Symptomatic lesions: surgical resection; seizure

Emerging: Stereotactic radiosurgery; beta-blockers/propranolol

name: Arteriovenous Malformations (AVM) — Cerebral
description: Abnormal tangles of arteries and veins bypassing capillary system; hemorrhage risk ~2–4% per year; most present in childhood.

frequency.global: ~20,000 – ~27,000 US: ~2,900 – ~4,400 US pediatric cases | Global: ~115,000 – ~175,000 global pediatric cases ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — AVM birth prevalence ~1/100,000/yr detected; pediatric ~10% of AVM population; unruptured AVM hemorrhage risk 2– 3%/yr; pediatric AVM hemorrhage risk higher than adults (~10–20%/yr vs 2– 4%); ARUBA trial excludes unruptured AVMs in children; multimodal Rx

Microsurgical resection; stereotactic radiosurgery

Emerging: Observation for unruptured low-grade; ARUBA trial
insights

name: Vein of Galen Malformation
description: Rare congenital arteriovenous malformation of the deep ventricular vein causing high- output cardiac failure in neonates and hydrocephalus.

frequency.global: ~2,000 – ~2,700 US: ~50 – ~150 new US cases/yr | Global: ~2,000 – ~5,000 new global cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — NORD; Vein of Galen malformation (VOGM) is rare arteriovenous fistula; ~1% of all pediatric brain AVMs; ~30% of all neonatal brain AVMs; presents neonatally with high-output cardiac failure; treatment: endovascular embolization

Endovascular embolization (staged, neonatal) —

Emerging: Timing optimization protocols; neonatal

name: CARASIL / CADASIL — Pediatric-Onset
description: Hereditary cerebrovascular disease with early strokes, white matter disease, and dementia; CADASIL from NOTCH3 mutations.

frequency.global: ~46,000 – ~92,000 US: ~5 – ~20 total US pediatric cases estimated | Global: ~100 – ~300 total global pediatric cases Insufficent Data : Estimates based on — CADASIL/CARASIL pediatric-onset is exceptionally rare; case reports only; CARASIL caused by HTRA1 mutation; few dozen global pediatric cases in literature; robust pediatric population data unavailable

Antiplatelet therapy; cardiovascular risk reduction;

Emerging: No disease-modifying therapy; NOTCH3 modifier

name: Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis
description: Most common autoimmune encephalitis; NR1 antibodies causing psychosis, seizures, movement disorder, and autonomic instability; often paraneoplastic.

frequency.global: ~2,300 – ~4,600 US: ~600 – ~1,500 new US pediatric cases/yr | Global: ~24,000 – ~60,000 new global cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — Dalmau et al. name: Anti-LGI1 / Anti-CASPR2 Encephalitis
description: Autoimmune limbic encephalitis with LGI1 antibodies (faciobrachial dystonic seizures, hyponatremia) or CASPR2 antibodies.

Emerging: Rituximab for refractory; long-term

name: MOG Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD)
description: MOG-IgG causing optic neuritis, ADEM, and transverse myelitis; distinct from MS and NMOSD; often monophasic in children.

name: Pediatric Multiple Sclerosis (Pediatric-Onset MS)
description: Relapsing-remitting demyelinating disease with onset before age 18; ~3–5% of all MS cases.

interferons/glatiramer

Emerging: High-efficacy: ocrelizumab/ofatumumab,

name: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
description: Post-infectious or post- vaccination multifocal demyelination with encephalopathy; usually monophasic in children.

frequency.global: ~6,900 – ~14,000 US: ~290 – ~1,000 new US pediatric cases/yr | Global: ~11,600 – ~40,000 new global cases/yr ✓ VERIFIED [CONFIRMED] — Pohl et al. IV methylprednisolone; rehabilitation; bladder

treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Rituximab for refractory; efgartigimod (Vyvgart)
FDA 2023 for adults

name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS / AIDP / AMAN / MFS)

IVIG (2g/kg over 2–5 days) — first-line; plasmapheresis

treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Complement inhibition trials; eculizumab for
refractory GBS

name: Cerebral Palsy — Dyskinetic, Spastic, Ataxic Subtypes

Spasticity: baclofen (oral/intrathecal), botulinum toxin;
SDR for spastic diplegia
treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Dystonia: trihexyphenidyl, tetrabenazine; DBS for
severe dyskinetic CP; exoskeleton rehab

treatment.emerging:
Emerging: Valbenazine (FDA adult, 2023);
fluphenazine/haloperidol/pimozide; DBS for severe TS

Emerging: Idebenone; no FDA-approved therapy;

Emerging: Genetic counseling + folic acid prophylaxis for
